title: Pharmacy Law, Ethics and Practice
description: Legal framework of pharmacy practice in Nigeria, regulatory agencies, drug classification and control, professional ethics, and community pharmacy practice.

topics.title: Pharmacy Legislation in Nigeria
topics.summary: The PCN Act 2022, registration and licensing, premises and regulatory offences.

notes.b: The Pharmacy Council of Nigeria (PCN) regulates the education, training and practice of pharmacy. The Pharmacy Council of Nigeria (Establishment) Act 2022 replaced the Pharmacists Council of Nigeria Act (Cap P17 LFN 2004). PCN functions include: registering and licensing pharmacists (annual licence renewal with mandatory continuing professional development — MCPD), registering pharmacy technicians and patent and proprietary medicine vendors (PPMVs), accrediting pharmacy schools and internship sites, registering and inspecting pharmaceutical premises (community pharmacies, hospital pharmacies, wholesale, manufacturing), and discipline through the Pharmacists Investigating Panel and the Pharmacists Disciplinary Tribunal. Every registered pharmacy must be under the supervision of a superintendent pharmacist. A one-year internship is required before full registration.

Other key laws: the NAFDAC Act (Cap N1 LFN 2004) — registration and control of drugs, food, cosmetics, medical devices and chemicals; the Food, Drugs and Related Products (Registration, etc.) Act; the Counterfeit and Fake Drugs and Unwholesome Processed Foods (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act — offences for manufacturing, selling or distributing fake drugs and selling drugs in unregistered premises (e.g. open markets); the Poisons and Pharmacy Act (Cap P6) — historical classification of poisons; the Dangerous Drugs Act (Cap D1) and NDLEA Act — narcotic control; and the National Health Act 2014. The National Drug Distribution Guidelines (NDDG) restrict sale of medicines to coordinated wholesale centres, aiming to close open drug markets such as Idumota (Lagos), Onitsha Bridgehead and Kano Sabon Gari.

topics.title: Drug Regulation and Controlled Substances
topics.summary: NAFDAC registration, drug classification (POM, P, OTC), controlled drugs and records.

notes.b: NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control, established 1993) registers regulated products (each gets a NAFDAC registration number), inspects manufacturing (GMP), controls imports and exports, tests quality, and conducts pharmacovigilance and post-marketing surveillance. Anti-counterfeiting tools include the Mobile Authentication Service (MAS — scratch-and-text codes), TruScan handheld spectrometers and Black Eye. Medicines are classified by access: Prescription-Only Medicines (POM — dispensed only on a valid prescription, e.g. antibiotics, antihypertensives), Pharmacy medicines (P — sold only in pharmacies under pharmacist supervision) and Over-the-Counter / General Sales List medicines (OTC — e.g. paracetamol in small packs; PPMVs may sell only OTC medicines on their approved list). Dispensing antibiotics without prescription contributes to antimicrobial resistance.

Narcotic and psychotropic substances are controlled under the Dangerous Drugs Act, NDLEA Act and international conventions (Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs 1961, Convention on Psychotropic Substances 1971, 1988 Convention against Illicit Traffic). The Federal Ministry of Health (through its Narcotics Control) and NAFDAC issue import permits and estimates to the International Narcotics Control Board (INCB). Pharmacies must keep a controlled drugs register recording each receipt and supply (date, name and address, prescriber, quantity, balance), store controlled drugs in a locked cabinet, and dispose of expired stock under supervision. Nigeria has low access to opioids for pain relief yet high misuse of tramadol and codeine; codeine-containing cough syrup importation was banned in 2018, and tramadol above 100 mg was banned.

topics.title: Professional Ethics
topics.summary: Code of ethics, principles of biomedical ethics, confidentiality and professional conduct.

notes.b: The four principles of biomedical ethics (Beauchamp and Childress): autonomy (respect patients' informed choices), beneficence (act for the patient's good), non-maleficence (do no harm) and justice (fair distribution of resources and equal treatment). Additional duties: veracity (truth-telling), fidelity and confidentiality. The PCN Code of Ethics for Pharmacists in Nigeria requires pharmacists to make the patient's well-being their first concern, maintain competence, respect confidentiality, avoid conflicts of interest, refrain from advertising in misleading ways, refuse to supply medicines where misuse is suspected, collaborate with other health professionals, and uphold the dignity of the profession. Consent must be informed and voluntary.

Common ethical dilemmas: requests for medicines without prescription (e.g. antibiotics, abortifacients), suspected prescription errors (the pharmacist must contact the prescriber rather than dispense or silently alter), confidentiality with HIV-positive patients versus partner protection, conscientious objection (e.g. to emergency contraception — must refer the patient elsewhere without delay), inducements from pharmaceutical companies, and dispensing in emergencies. Professional misconduct includes dispensing without a licence, allowing unqualified staff to dispense unsupervised, selling fake or expired drugs, falsifying records and bringing the profession into disrepute. The pharmacist's oath and the Pharmaceutical Society of Nigeria (PSN — the professional association, distinct from the regulator PCN) promote standards.

topics.title: Community Pharmacy Practice
topics.summary: Dispensing process, prescription requirements, counselling, and public health roles.

notes.b: A valid prescription includes: patient's name, age (and weight for children), address; date; drug name (preferably generic), strength, dosage form, dose, frequency, duration and quantity; prescriber's name, signature and registration details. The dispensing process: receive and validate the prescription (legality, clinical appropriateness, interactions, allergies), prepare and select the product, label (patient name, drug, strength, directions in clear language, date, pharmacy name, warnings), perform a final check, and counsel the patient. Good dispensing practice includes clean premises, correct storage (temperature, light), first-expiry-first-out (FEFO) stock rotation, and record keeping (prescription records, controlled drugs register). Pictograms and local languages help patients with low literacy.

Community pharmacists are often the first point of contact for health care in Nigeria. Roles: responding to symptoms (with referral when red flags are present — WWHAM questions: Who, What symptoms, How long, Action taken, Medication), screening (blood pressure, blood glucose, BMI), health promotion (smoking cessation, weight management), family planning services, malaria testing with RDTs before ACT treatment, HIV testing and PrEP support, immunisation (in some settings), medicines use review, antimicrobial stewardship and pharmacovigilance reporting. Business management covers procurement from licensed wholesalers, pricing, inventory control (ABC/VEN analysis), staff management and compliance with PCN inspections.

topics.title: Hospital and Institutional Pharmacy
topics.summary: Drug and therapeutics committees, formulary management, drug distribution systems and aseptic services.

notes.b: Hospital pharmacy departments manage procurement, storage, distribution and rational use of medicines. The Drug and Therapeutics Committee (DTC), including doctors, pharmacists and nurses, develops and maintains the hospital formulary (list of approved medicines, based on the national Essential Medicines List), treatment guidelines and antimicrobial policies, and monitors adverse drug reactions and medication errors. Drug distribution systems: floor stock (ward stock — convenient but error-prone and prone to wastage), individual patient prescription, and unit-dose dispensing (each dose packaged and labelled — fewer errors, less waste). The Drug Revolving Fund (DRF) in Nigerian public hospitals uses sales income to replenish stock, improving availability.

Aseptic services prepare sterile products — parenteral nutrition, cytotoxic chemotherapy and IV admixtures — in controlled environments (laminar airflow cabinets, isolators, cleanrooms) with trained staff and validated procedures; cytotoxic handling requires biological safety cabinets, PPE and spill kits. Clinical pharmacy services on wards include medication reconciliation, therapeutic drug monitoring, and ward rounds. Medication error prevention: tall-man lettering (e.g. hydrOXYzine vs hydrALAZINE), separating look-alike sound-alike drugs, independent double checks for high-alert medicines (insulin, potassium chloride concentrate, anticoagulants, opioids, chemotherapy), and a non-punitive reporting culture. Emergency preparedness includes crash-cart stocking and antidote availability.
